title: Ramsey Party Lesson
plainSentence: A lesson that lets you colour the lines between six dots red or blue and discover why a one-colour triangle can never be avoided.
pitch: Six dots, fifteen lines, two colours: you try to colour every line so that no triangle is all one colour, first on five dots (it works) and then on six (it never does). A guided ladder turns your failed attempts into the proof, so the pigeonhole argument feels obvious rather than memorised, and a final rung shows how fast the same question becomes impossible to settle by hand.
firstMinute: The first frame shows five dots in a ring with a red pentagon and a blue star already drawn and the words 'no one-colour triangle here'. A button adds a sixth dot; its new lines appear grey, and as the visitor taps lines to colour them, a glowing triangle flashes the moment one colour closes a triangle. First success: the visitor makes a triangle appear on six dots within seconds and cannot make it go away.
conceptsToLearn: A line between two dots can be red (the two people know each other) or blue (they are strangers)
whyNow: Timeless: a short, complete proof with a surprising edge (five is not enough, six is), and nothing like it in the build history. It also gives the pool a combinatorics lesson that is not about primes or number systems.

purposeDetail.concept: Ramsey's party problem: in any group of six people, either three of them all know each other or three of them are all strangers. Colouring the 15 pairs of a complete graph on six dots with two colours always leaves a one-colour triangle (R(3,3) = 6), while five dots can be coloured with none (a red pentagon and a blue pentagram).
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Most explanations state the pigeonhole step in one sentence and move on, so learners accept the result without feeling why a fifth dot's colouring escapes but the sixth's cannot. Being allowed to try, fail and see exactly which line closes the trap is what the page adds.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious teenagers and adults with no maths beyond school; teachers looking for a ten-minute proof activity.
misconceptions: Checking a few colourings and finding a triangle each time counts as a proof (it does not; the page contrasts a few tries with the exhaustive argument)
Showing six is enough also shows five is not (the lower bound needs its own example: the pentagon and pentagram colouring)
Red and blue mean friends versus enemies (they only mean know each other versus do not)
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Pick one dot. It has five lines, and two colours cannot share five lines without one colour getting three. Look at the three dots at the far ends: any line among them in that colour makes a triangle with your dot, and if none is, they form a triangle in the other colour. Every escape route is closed.
demos: Rung 1: five dots with the pentagon and pentagram colouring already drawn; tap lines to try to break it and see that you cannot make a triangle without redrawing
Rung 2: add a sixth dot and try to colour its five new lines without making a triangle; a live hint highlights the line that always loses
Rung 3: pick any dot; its five lines fall into two colour bins and the bins visibly overflow at three (the pigeonhole step)
Rung 4: the three far-end dots light up and the visitor checks the three lines among them, ending in a red or a blue triangle in every case

Rung 5: a quilt view lays the 15 line colours out as a strip of 15 patches; a shuffle button tries thousands of random colourings and counts how many triangles each has, and the count never reaches zero
Rung 6: the same question with four-dot groups on 17 dots, shown as a pre-drawn colouring where no one-colour four-group exists, to feel why the next case is out of reach by hand
checkQuestions: Pick a dot on a seven-person party. How many lines leave it, and what is the least number that must share a colour?
On five people, colour the lines so that no one-colour triangle exists. Which two shapes do the colours draw?
Why does a single colouring of six dots that happens to contain a red triangle not prove the general statement?
If the lines among the three far-end dots are all blue, what triangle have you found?

research.summary: The statement, the pigeonhole proof and the pentagon-pentagram counterexample for five points appear in lecture notes, a maths-society blog and a problem-solving wiki, so the core is textbook-solid. The extension to four-person groups is also documented: a self-complementary colouring of 17 points with no one-colour four-group is the standard witness that 18 is needed. The whole claim for six dots is small enough (2 to the 15th = 32,768 colourings) that the page can ship a script-checked exhaustive count, so the lesson does not rest on search snippets alone. The idea of the minimum number of one-colour triangles in a six-dot colouring is attributed to Goodman in one search result only and is kept as optional.

facts.claim: Any red/blue colouring of the 15 lines between six dots contains a triangle of one colour (R(3,3)=6); the proof picks one dot, notes three of its five lines share a colour, and checks the lines among their far ends.
Five dots can be coloured with no one-colour triangle: sides of a pentagon in one colour and its diagonals (the pentagram) in the other, so six is the smallest number that forces a triangle.
R(4,4)=18: a two-colouring of 17 points exists (differences that are squares modulo 17 in one colour) with no one-colour group of four, and 18 points always force one.

Every red/blue colouring of the lines between six dots has at least two one-colour triangles (Goodman, case of six). Single search result; the page can instead show a count computed by the page's own exhaustive check.
Learners commonly check only the upper bound (six is enough) and skip the lower bound (five is not). Reported by a search summary of a college handout, not confirmed on the page.

inspirations: Ramsey's party problem as taught in discrete maths courses

design.coreLoop: Colour lines, watch the trap close, ask 'where is the escape', get the hint that names the dot with three same-coloured lines, then answer a check question. Each rung changes one thing (5 dots, 6 dots, the pigeonhole bins, the far-end triangle, a bulk shuffle), so the ladder keeps feeling like one idea getting clearer.
sophisticationHooks: A live pigeonhole view that groups the chosen dot's five lines into red and blue bins and flags the overfull bin
An exhaustive checker over all 32,768 colourings of six dots, run in a worker, which proves the claim in front of the visitor and lists the minimum number of triangles found
A quilt view that lays all 15 line colours out as a patch strip, so symmetry and the pentagon-pentagram pattern show as a repeat
A top rung that loads the 17-dot colouring and lets the visitor verify no one-colour four-group by a guided search
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: one SVG board with 5 to 6 dots, tap-to-colour lines, triangle highlighter, pigeonhole bins view, quilt strip, exhaustive checker, 6 guided rungs with 4 check questions, a short written explainer. Cut: seven or more dots beyond the single 17-dot display, user-entered graphs, accounts, sharing.
risks: The 'learners skip the lower bound' misconception comes from one search summary (verified:false); the page should phrase it as a general caution rather than a measured fact, or leave it out.
The minimum-two-triangles result is in one search result only (verified:false); the page should show the count computed in the browser, labelled as checked here.
The exact value of R(5,5) was not confirmed to a specific bound in the results seen (older bounds were quoted), so the page says only 'not known' with a dated source, or leaves it out.
Engineering: the 17-dot rung must be hand-checked by a script before shipping so the displayed colouring is truly free of one-colour four-groups.
Risk of looking like a puzzle game: keep the framing as a guided proof with questions, not a score.
